## Why AI works {.dark-slide background-color="#1a3a5c"}

__A nonlinear tour of large language models__

::: {.big-claim}
Think of a language model as a nonlinear dynamical system. Small changes can produce disproportionately large effects.
:::

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">Linear intuition</span>

Double the input and you roughly double the output.

<br>

The system is comparatively easy to predict.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Nonlinear behavior</span>

Output feeds back into the system.

<br>

A small change can produce a large effect, while a large change can produce almost no effect.
</div>
</div>


::: {.source-note}
Adapted from Thomas Cherickal, “The Nonlinear Science Behind Large Language Models,” HackerNoon, September 9, 2026.
Article sections: “Nobody Knows How These Things Work” and “What Is a Nonlinear Dynamical System?”
:::

---

## Training follows a power law

The article begins with the most reliable pattern in modern AI: as we add parameters, data, and compute, prediction error falls in a smooth but expensive curve.

<div class="formula">
Loss = unavoidable error + model-size penalty + data-size penalty
</div>

<br>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">What scales</span>

More parameters give a model more capacity. More training text gives it more patterns to learn.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Why it matters</span>

Doubling the model does not double its quality. Each additional gain requires much more data and compute.
</div>
</div>

::: {.big-claim}
The 20-to-1 rule: roughly 20 training tokens per parameter is a useful compute-optimal target.
:::

::: {.source-note}
Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models; Hoffmann et al. (2022), Chinchilla. Numbers summarized by the article.
:::

---

## Smooth training can produce sudden skills {.dark-slide background-color="#1a3a5c"}

The loss curve may improve gradually while a real-world capability appears almost all at once.

<div class="sequence">
<div>
<strong>Below the threshold</strong>
<span>Arithmetic or reasoning looks like random guessing.</span>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Near the threshold</strong>
<span>A small change in scale, data, or training can matter a lot.</span>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Above the threshold</strong>
<span>The capability becomes useful and feels like a jump.</span>
</div>
</div>

<br>

Physics calls this a **phase transition**: water stays liquid, then changes state at a critical temperature. The article argues that some AI abilities behave similarly.

::: {.discussion}
Question: When a skill appears suddenly, did the model “learn” it gradually underneath, or did something genuinely new emerge?
:::

::: {.source-note}
Wei et al. (2022); Schaeffer et al. (2023); Du et al. (2024). The article notes that some emergence claims depend on how we measure ability.
:::

---

## Grokking: memorization gives way to a rule

**Grokking** is a delayed jump from memorizing training examples to discovering a rule that generalizes to examples the model has never seen.

Researchers saw this in small models trained on modular arithmetic, such as clock math where 9 + 5 = 2 on a 12-hour clock. The model first fit the examples, then seemed stuck, then suddenly found the underlying pattern.

<div class="sequence">
<div>
<strong>Memorize</strong>
<span>Seen examples are correct. New examples fail.</span>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Plateau</strong>
<span>Training continues while test performance appears unchanged. Internally, a better strategy may be forming.</span>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Generalize</strong>
<span>The model finds a compact rule that works on new cases.</span>
</div>
</div>

<br>

::: {.big-claim}
Understanding can be simpler inside the network than memorizing every answer.
:::

::: {.source-note}
Power et al. (2022), “Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting”; Nanda et al. (2023); Varma et al. (2023). Article section: “Why does this happen?”
:::

---

## The useful zone sits near the edge

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">Temperature</span>

In an LLM, temperature is a sampling setting that controls how much variety the model allows when choosing its next token.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Criticality</span>

Criticality is the boundary between rigid order and unstable chaos: sensitive enough for rich patterns, stable enough to preserve signal.
</div>
</div>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">Low temperature: too orderly</span>

Near-zero temperature favors the most likely continuation. Output can become repetitive and dull.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">High temperature: too chaotic</span>

High temperature spreads probability across more alternatives. Output can become fluent, confident nonsense.
</div>
</div>

<br>

::: {.big-claim}
Useful output lives between repetition and randomness.
:::

::: {.source-note}
Schoenholz et al. (2017); Dong et al. (2021); Bertschinger and Natschläger (2004). Article sections: “At the Edge of Chaos” and “Self-organized criticality.”
:::

---

## In-context learning switches on {.compact-slide}

::: {.big-claim}
In-context learning means using examples in the prompt to infer a pattern without changing the model’s weights.
:::

For example: show “red = warm” and “blue = cool,” then ask the model to classify “green.” The model adapts inside the conversation, without retraining.

The article highlights research suggesting that this ability appears after roughly **2.5 to 5 billion training tokens**, across a wide range of model sizes.

::: {.big-claim}
The prompt may be the same. The model may have crossed a training threshold.
:::

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">Before</span>

Examples in the prompt do little more than provide extra text.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">After</span>

Induction-head circuits are transformer attention patterns that spot a repeated sequence and copy what followed.
</div>
</div>

::: {.source-note}
Olsson et al. (2022), “In-Context Learning and Induction Heads”; Zhu et al. (2024). Article section: “The most beautiful result in the field.”
:::

---

## Language lives on a thinner shape than it occupies

<div class="image-layout">
<div>
<img src="manifold-article-image.png" alt="Fractal triangle illustration from the article, labeled with model scaling thresholds" />
<small>Illustration from the article</small>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Manifold hypothesis</span>

High-dimensional data often lies near a much thinner, lower-dimensional structure.

<br>

Think of a crumpled sheet: it occupies three-dimensional space, but the sheet itself is two-dimensional. Images and word embeddings may work similarly inside their enormous spaces.

<div class="formula">
Space around the data ≠ complexity of the data
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: {.source-note}
Sharma and Kaplan (2020); Kaplan et al. (2020). Image from [the article](https://hackernoon.com/the-nonlinear-science-behind-large-language-models), which identifies its images as AI-generated.
:::

---

## What this lens helps us notice {.dark-slide background-color="#2a6f97"}

The nonlinear-dynamics lens does not make every AI claim true. It gives us better questions:

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">Ask about thresholds</span>

What changed: model size, training data, loss, prompt, or measurement?

<br>

Did a capability appear, or did our scoring method reveal it differently?
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Ask about generalization</span>

Did the model memorize an answer, or discover a method that works on new cases?

<br>

What evidence would distinguish those explanations?
</div>
</div>

<br>

::: {.discussion}
For a small group: choose one AI capability and identify its possible threshold, evidence, and failure mode.
:::

::: {.source-note}
Synthesis of the article’s discussion of scaling, emergence, grokking, criticality, and scientific testing.
:::

---

## The biggest question points back to us

The article’s most speculative move is also its most memorable: LLMs may be the first complex nonlinear systems that are fully instrumented.

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<span class="label">What we can do with models</span>

Read every weight. Save every training checkpoint. Change one variable and rerun the experiment.
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">What we cannot do with brains</span>

We cannot inspect every connection or replay a human mind with one controlled change.
</div>
</div>

<br>

The author is careful not to claim that an LLM is a brain. The proposal is narrower: studying emergence in models might give us tools for studying emergence in minds.

::: {.discussion}
What would count as evidence that a model has discovered a rule rather than memorized an answer?
:::

::: {.source-note}
Article conclusion: “What if the science we develop to understand emergence in language models becomes the science that finally cracks emergence in minds?”
:::
